lectures.title: Volumes vs Partitions: Mounting and Accessing Storage

cues.en: In this lecture, we want to have a look at how we can mount a volume.
But before we can have a look at that, we need to clarify the the term volume.
What is a volume?
So far we have talked a lot about partitions.
Those were parts of our physical drive and they allowed us to create those areas on our drive that then
could be separated from other parts of that drive.
So for example, we could have one partition for the one operating system and another partition for
another one or another partition for backups.
So this was a partition, but now we are talking about volumes.
A volume is slightly often it refers to the same thing and theory, but it means something slightly
different.
It's more a logical storage unit on our computer that we can use.
So usually when we have a partition and we create a file system on that one, then we have a volume
because this is then a logical storage unit on our computer are those logical storage units, and they
usually appear as an accessible drive or partition.
Why did I say usually here?
Well, imagine we have a file system that our operating system doesn't support.
In that case, of course it wouldn't appear.
But as long as everything is supported and it's mounted, this is what we'll have a look at in this
lecture.
Correctly, it will appear as an accessible drive and we can access this volume from our computer.
The distinction between partition and volume is especially important because a volume can be even more
abstract than a partition.
A partition was just this physical.
This part of a physical drive.
A volume is a usable space where we can store files somewhere.
And this is important because a volume can be more than just a partition with a file system.
This is because there's, for example, this logical volume manager.
That's a separate chapter here in this course where we can combine multiple partitions, even from different
drives into one logical volume so we can have one file system spanning multiple physical drives.
And if this is one file system on our computer, it's just one volume that is running on multiple drives,
for example.
So there's a distinction here that with those logical volumes, more on those in a later chapter or
another example would be that a volume could also be stored on another computer and then only accessed
through the network.

that one.
Maybe there's a partition somewhere on another computer.
